endorsements.quote: Continuous monitoring of deployed AI systems should become standard practice to detect performance drift early.
Continuous surveillance should detect deviations from expected behavior and trigger corrective actions promptly.

Bias mitigation must also extend beyond the development phase: continuous auditing and multidisciplinary oversight involving ethicists, clinicians, and data scientists are necessary to identify emergent biases and sustain fairness.
Models should be trained on datasets that are diverse and representative of the populations they serve.
Another critical step is eliminating proxy variables that encode protected attributes, such as race or socioeconomic status.

Institutions should adopt phased implementation to distribute costs and workload, whereas policymakers establish funding mechanisms that support infrastructure, data curation, and workforce development.
Second, comprehensive training programs should emphasize both the capabilities and limitations of AI, helping clinicians critically interpret system outputs and maintain accountability.
Health care institutions should complement academic reform with ongoing, role-specific professional training that balances theoretical understanding with hands-on experience.
Hospitals should establish internal ethics committees to oversee AI procurement and usage decisions, ensuring these are guided by patient safety and clinical benefit rather than commercial interest.
Independent auditing of AI trials and deployment outcomes should be routine to identify potential biases.
Addressing these challenges requires formalized, multidisciplinary collaboration throughout design, testing, and deployment.
Development teams should include health care providers, patients, ethicists, data scientists, and engineers to foster trust, ownership, and shared accountability.
Evidence-based frameworks should guide the selection of use cases that address measurable clinical or operational needs.
Developers should assess existing technological infrastructure before deployment to ensure compatibility and minimize operational disruption.
Over time, national and international frameworks should evolve toward shared responsibility models that clearly delineate obligations across clinicians, institutions, and AI developers.
Establishing regulatory and technical guidance for conducting AI-specific RCTs is crucial for ensuring that models undergo testing under real-world conditions.
To improve generalizability, models should be trained and validated on datasets from multiple institutions and populations, using both cross-validation and external validation techniques.

unlisted_practices: Establish standardized international regulatory and governance frameworks harmonized across regulators.
Require regulatory approval of health care AI by independent bodies analogous to drugs and medical devices before clinical deployment.
Embed confidence assessment mechanisms so models do not generate outputs when uncertainty exceeds safe thresholds.
Implement fail-safe measures to prevent unreliable AI predictions from influencing clinical decisions.
Use AI strictly as decision support rather than autonomous decision-maker, with ultimate responsibility remaining with clinicians.
Legally require notifying patients whenever AI is used in their care and provide clear explanations of how it works, its data use, and risks.
Use dynamic consent models and let patients refuse AI involvement in their care.
Mandate disclosure of all financial ties between clinicians, institutions, and AI developers.
Reform medical and health sciences curricula to include core AI competencies.
Fund equitable AI deployment and infrastructure in low-resource settings and develop cost-effective open-source AI.
Adopt interoperability standards such as FHIR and OMOP for AI integration with EHRs.
Establish structured feedback loops between clinicians and developers to inform retraining and improvement.
Use shadow-clinician immersion to understand workflows when designing AI tools.
Create centralized anonymized data repositories to support longitudinal and prospective AI validation.
Use open reporting of algorithms, datasets, and validation outcomes to enable peer scrutiny.
Mandate public reporting of AI outcomes and performance auditing by regulators.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/framework commentary paper offering recommendations for systemic, regulatory, educational, and ethical integration of AI into clinical workflows.
